extracted.intended_audience: advanced students, researchers, and philosophers interested in the foundations and epistemology of mechanics (physicists, historians/philosophers of science)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for forming and assessing physical concepts and systems of mechanics (laws, definitions like mass, the role of force, variational principles, reference frames). Aimed at judging conceptual clarity, empirical grounding, and methodological economy in mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of measurement (unit convention vs numeric result)
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of the unit of measurement is convention; the number of measurement is a result of inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Units are conventional decisions, whereas the numerical relations derived from measurement are empirical results found by inquiry. Example: calling the negative inverse ratio of mutually induced accelerations the 'mass-ratio' is a convention, but that those ratios are independent of the kind and order of combination of bodies is an empirical result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish conventions from empirical results in defining inertial systems
rubrics_metrics.description: A coordinate system in which three material points move in straight lines is a simple convention; whether a fourth free point will also move in a straight line with respect to that system is a result of inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing definitions or coordinate conventions (e.g., Lange's inertial system built from three points), explicitly separate what is stipulated by definition from what must be checked empirically. The empirical status (e.g., universality of straight-line motion for other bodies) must be established by observation/experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference frames should be grounded in astronomical/time standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer the law of inertia, with respect to space, to the fixed stars and, with respect to time, to the rotation of the earth as a tolerably accurate approximation until future experience provides corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mach argues that consideration of fixed stars and Earth's rotation provided the historical basis for the law of inertia; excluding the rest of the world (isolated points) is inadmissible. Use astronomical benchmarks as pragmatic reference frames while allowing for refinement from future observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hertz's criteria for scientific concepts (logical admissibility, correctness, appropriateness, economy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive images (concepts) should be chosen so that the consequences which necessarily follow from them in thought agree with the consequences which necessarily follow from them in nature; they must be logically admissible (free from self-contradictions), correct (conform to relations obtaining between objects), and appropriate, containing the least possible superfluous features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate theories by (1) internal logical consistency, (2) empirical correctness, and (3) parsimony/appropriateness. Mach notes these requirements and equates 'appropriateness' with the criterion of economy; concepts are not formed arbitrarily but are shaped by adapting ideas to the sensuous environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid logically defective expositions; be precise about force and mass
rubrics_metrics.description: Expositions must avoid logical defects such as double-counting inertia (e.g., treating inertia both as mass and again as a force); clarity in defining 'force' and its role is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticisms that 'force' is unclear apply only to defective presentations, not necessarily to the concepts themselves. Historical figures (Huygens, Newton) handled these points clearly; modern expositions should likewise avoid introducing contradictions or redundant attributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret variational/minimum principles non-teleologically
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimum (variational) principles do not imply purpose or teleology; their import is of a different property than that of purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using principles of least action/least constraint, read them as mathematical/dynamical conditions characterizing the actual motion (e.g., uniqueness of dynamically determined motion), not as implying foresight or final causes. Mach emphasizes that reference to the future is unavoidable in time concepts but does not equate to teleology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of differential equations over ontological interpretation (force vs connexion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether one interprets interactions as forces or as connexions (hidden masses/motions), the essential, experience-established fact is the existence of linear differential equations between the coordinates of the masses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus evaluation on the mathematical description (differential equations) that captures observed dependencies of motions; ontological labels (force, connexion, hidden masses) are interpretive and secondary so long as the equations reproduce experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of actual motion from minimum/variational principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimum conditions do not presuppose purpose; they imply that the actual motion is dynamically determined and unique — deviations are not present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a formulation by whether it yields a unique dynamically determined motion (Mach cites Lagrange's equations/Hertz's principle). References: Petzoldt on the 'law of uniqueness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical formalism must not replace physical content
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal mathematical system (e.g., Hertz's ideal form) may shrink the apparent physical content; the physical side of mechanical problems is not disposed of by formal elaboration and must be separately addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging theories, distinguish between mathematical adequacy and physical explanatory content: a beautiful formalism must still account for empirical physical principles and experiences that give it content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define mass dynamically (by accelerations) not as quantity of matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass should be defined by the dynamical relationships (mutual accelerations) bodies determine in one another; mass is a dynamical concept, not merely 'quantity of matter'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mach defends defining mass via accelerations so that measurement by weight follows naturally; avoid circular constructions that presuppose force or quantity of matter. This definition resists critiques that it tacitly assumes a single force acting on both masses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the law of inertia as empirically grounded, not a priori certain
rubrics_metrics.description: Any deduction of the law of inertia from a general principle (like causality) is inadmissible; the law has an empirical origin with possibly a supra-empirical element (e.g., reference to absolute space), and should be seen as a tolerably accurate approximation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims of axiomatic certainty skeptically; regard inertia as informed by experience and reference choices (fixed stars, earth's rotation). Consider positions of Heymans, Poske, Petzoldt: empirical input determines phenomena, then uniqueness follows when data are adequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation and coherence of scientific concepts to sensory environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Concepts are formed consciously and purposely but are outcomes of an endeavour to adapt ideas to the sensuous environment; agreement of concepts with one another is a logically necessary requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess concepts for how well they fit sensory/experimental data and for internal coherence. Mach notes that logical necessity is the only necessity we have knowledge of, and that empirical refutation can always overturn assumed adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ad hoc hypotheses; require physical demonstrability
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptions such as space-as-medium should have properties demonstrable physically and not be assumed ad hoc; otherwise, preference should be given to simpler assumptions tied to observed accelerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing explanatory devices (mediums, hidden masses/motions), require that their properties be empirically demonstrable or else prefer direct reference to observed accelerations. Example: Budde's conception of space as a medium is acceptable only if its properties can be shown physically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate methodological convention from empirical generalisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodical devices (e.g., coordinate choices, imaginings) are conventions to facilitate exposition, but broad empirical generalisations must be justified by experience and not conflated with definitional choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating presentations, note when a device is adopted for methodical advantages (simplicity, perspicuity) versus when a claim is being made about nature. Mach cautions against confusing the two (e.g., Lange's coordinate formulation is methodically attractive but may implicitly rely on fixed stars).
